title: First move after being scammed
prompt: You realize you just gave your card number to a scammer 15 minutes ago. What should you do first?

options.label: Call your bank immediately using the number on the back of your card.
Search online for an asset recovery service to trace the stolen money.

reasons.opt-bank: Calling your bank right away can freeze the card, reverse pending charges, and protect your account from more loss.
reasons.opt-search: Online "recovery companies" are second-wave scammers who take upfront fees and recover nothing.

explanation: In the first hour after a scam, speed is everything. Call your bank or card issuer using the phone number printed on your card. They can freeze cards, dispute charges, and secure your account.
takeaways: Call your bank immediately using the number on your card.
Beware of fake online recovery services.

title: First hour after sending money
prompt: You just sent money to someone you now suspect was a scammer. Put the first-hour steps in order:
steps: Gather receipts, transaction dates, and the scammer's contact details.
Call your bank or card company's fraud department right away to cancel or freeze the transfer.
File an official fraud report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Tell a trusted family member or friend so you have support and aren't dealing with it alone.
whyFirstStepMatters: Every minute counts when trying to stop an unauthorized transfer. Calling your bank immediately gives them the best chance of reversing a wire or freezing compromised cards before more money is lost.
explanation: In the first hour after losing money to a scammer, contacting your financial institution immediately gives you the best chance of reversing charges or freezing your accounts. Never wait.
takeaways: Call your bank immediately to stop transactions.
Keep receipts and records of all scam messages.

title: First hour after giving a password
prompt: You accidentally entered your main password on a look-alike fake website. Put these recovery steps in order:
steps: Turn on two-factor authentication (an extra verification code) on your account.
Change the password on that account right now from an official, safe device.
Check your recent login history and sign out of all active sessions.
Update any other accounts that used the same or a similar password.
whyFirstStepMatters: Changing your password immediately cuts off the scammer's access before they can lock you out by changing your recovery email or phone number.
explanation: When a password is leaked, act fast to change it before the scammer takes over your account. Then sign out other sessions and secure other accounts that shared the password.
takeaways: Never reuse the same password across multiple accounts.
